clinicalPearls: A chronic, low-grade, usually unilateral anterior uveitis that is characteristically white and painless, often discovered incidentally or when cataract reduces vision.
Diffuse, small, stellate keratic precipitates scattered across the whole corneal endothelium, rather than clustered inferiorly, are a hallmark.
Iris heterochromia results from stromal atrophy; the affected iris is typically hypochromic and lighter, though in brown irides the loss of the anterior stroma can make it appear darker.
Posterior synechiae are characteristically absent even after years of inflammation, an important distinguishing feature.
Fine iris and angle vessels are fragile, and a filiform anterior chamber haemorrhage on paracentesis or cataract surgery is the Amsler-Verrey sign.
Posterior subcapsular cataract and secondary open-angle glaucoma are the two principal complications.
An association with rubella virus, and in some regions cytomegalovirus, is increasingly recognised as an aetiological factor.
The inflammation responds poorly to and generally does not warrant long-term topical corticosteroids, which risk steroid-induced pressure rise without altering the course.
reference.pathophysiology: Fuchs uveitis is a chronic low-grade iridocyclitis characterised by diffuse iris stromal atrophy and depigmentation, mild persistent anterior chamber inflammation and abnormal fragile vasculature in the iris and anterior chamber angle. Progressive atrophy of the iris stroma and pigment epithelium produces the heterochromia and, on transillumination, diffuse thinning. Chronic low-grade inflammation, with lymphocytic infiltration and scattered stellate keratic precipitates, occurs without the fibrinous exudation that produces synechiae in other uveitides, which explains the notable absence of posterior synechiae. Rubella virus, and cytomegalovirus in some populations, has been implicated as a chronic antigenic stimulus. New fragile vessels in the angle and iris account for the tendency to hyphaema with minor trauma or surgery, and chronic trabecular involvement leads to secondary open-angle glaucoma.
additionalDifferentials: herpetic (herpes simplex or varicella-zoster) anterior uveitis
congenital or acquired Horner syndrome causing heterochromia
additionalInvestigations: slit-lamp examination for diffuse stellate keratic precipitates and absent synechiae
iris transillumination and comparison of iris colour between eyes
gonioscopy for fine angle vessels and pigmentation
intraocular pressure measurement and glaucoma work-up
aqueous polymerase chain reaction for rubella and cytomegalovirus in selected cases
optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve and perimetry when glaucoma is suspected
cataract assessment and biometry before surgery
redFlags: rising intraocular pressure signalling secondary glaucoma
spontaneous hyphaema or unexpected bleeding during surgery
atypical bilateral or granulomatous features suggesting an alternative diagnosis
rapid visual decline from dense posterior subcapsular cataract
reference.prognosis: The prognosis for vision is generally good, with cataract surgery usually well tolerated and effective; the main threat to sight is secondary glaucoma, which can be difficult to control and requires long-term monitoring.
pitfalls: Treating the low-grade inflammation with prolonged topical steroids, which add steroid-induced pressure rise without benefit.
Overlooking the diagnosis because the eye is white and painless and the patient asymptomatic.
Missing early secondary glaucoma, the principal cause of visual loss.
Being surprised by intraoperative filiform hyphaema during cataract surgery.
Misclassifying the unilateral heterochromia and cataract as another uveitic entity and instituting inappropriate immunosuppression.
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course, Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation
Standardisation of Uveitis Nomenclature classification criteria
management: Avoid unnecessary long-term topical corticosteroids, as the chronic low-grade inflammation responds poorly and rarely warrants aggressive immunosuppression
Reserve a short course of topical corticosteroid only for genuinely symptomatic inflammatory flares
Lower intraocular pressure with topical anti-glaucoma agents for secondary open-angle glaucoma, escalating to glaucoma surgery when medically uncontrolled
Offer cataract surgery for visually significant posterior subcapsular cataract, which is generally well tolerated
Anticipate fragile iris and angle vessels and the risk of intraoperative filiform haemorrhage (Amsler-Verrey sign) during surgery
Monitor intraocular pressure, optic nerve and visual fields long-term, as secondary glaucoma is the main threat to sight
Consider aqueous PCR for rubella or cytomegalovirus in atypical cases to support the diagnosis
